tathāvyavasthāpaka iti kathaṃ sidhyet,- ityāśaṅkāṃ (page 365) śamayan evam iti pūrvasūcitāṃ yuktimāha tatrāpi hi iti | vikalpāvasthāyāṃ hi yadi tādṛśāveva tau, tarhi pūrvamakṛtamidānīṃ kurutaḥ iti kaḥ pratīyāt | anyonyāpekṣayā hi prāgbhāvasya paścādbhāvasya ca yat vyavasthāpanaṃ, tat na upapadyate, tatastau dvāvapi svaviṣayamātraṃ spṛśataḥ | itthaṃtu etadupapadyate ityāha ekasmiṃstu iti | pratyakṣānupalambhapravāhapañcakena hi pañca tāni prameyāṇi ekasmin saṃvitsamudre pātyamānāni tatsvātantryataraṅgabalādanyonyāpekṣāmayāni ghaṭaḥ- paṭaḥ- itivat viviktābhāsavimarśavailakṣaṇyena [vibhaktā ka. |] bhāsyante vimṛśyante ca | tatra yo'sāvābhāsanavyāpārakṛtaḥ pañcānāmekābhāsaḥ, sa kāryakāraṇabhāvābhāsaḥ; tathāvimarśaśca pramātṛvyāpāraḥ | iyamevaca sā pramāṇayojanātmikā [pramāṇaprayojanātmikā ka. |] samastavyavahāropayoginī yuktirucyate, tadvyāpāravirahe pramāṇānyapi akiṃcitkarāṇyeva | tataśca uktaṃ parameśvareṇaiva śrīmukuṭasaṃhitāyāṃ saṃvidvyāpāra evaikā yuktiḥ sarvatra sādhanī | bhoge vāpyathavā mokṣe tenāsyāmādṛto bhavet || ityādi | sa ca yojaka eveti sarvamiṣṭaṃ siddham || 4 || nanu pratyakṣānupalambhairyadakāri, taccedekīkartavyamiti iyatā pramāturaṅgīkaraṇaṃ, tat kimanena, tadekīkaraṇe hi smṛtireva udyuṅkte ityāśaṅkya sūtraṃ smṛtau yaiva svasaṃvittiḥ pramāṇaṃ svātmasaṃbhave | pūrvānubhavasadbhāve sādhanaṃ saiva nāparam || 5 || pratyakṣānupalambharūpāṇi saṃvedanāni yadyat nijaṃ saṃvedyamagṛhṇan, tasya tāvat smaraṇe yat prakāśanaṃ, tat na smaraṇakālopanatamapūrvaṃ (page 366) gṛhītagrahaṇasvabhāvatvāt, apitu pūrvānubhava eva tat | sa ca idānīṃ pṛthak vedyatvena na nirbhāsate abhāvāt tasya, bhāve'pi vedyatvena bhāsane jñātajñānaṃ syāt; tat na smaraṇaṃ, nacāpi jñānaṃ jñānāntaravedyamiti darśitaṃ bahuśaḥ | tadasya sato'pi pṛthak svaprakāśatāyāmanyonyānanuṣaktaṃ saṃvedanadvayameva syāt, na smaraṇam | tadiyadaṅgīkartavyaṃ- yat smaraṇakāle'pi anubhavaḥ prācyo'ntaḥsvasaṃvedanātmā sanneva smṛtisvarūpasadbhāvāvedakasvasaṃvedanādabhinnaḥ pr
**The valid means is the knower's own operation** The saptamo vimarśa is establishing the one support of the powers. And its deepest point is that the valid means (pramāṇa) is not a separate instrument standing over against the knower. It is the knower's own operation (pramātṛ-vyāpāra) — the act by which the many cognitions are gathered into the one knower. The five objects of perception and non-perception, thrown into the one consciousness-ocean, are joined by the freedom-wave, becoming mutually dependent (jar and cloth, as it were); they shine with their distinct appearances and are re-reflected. The one appearance, made by the manifestation-operation of the five, is the cause-and-effect appearance; and the re-recollection is the knower's operation. This — the joining — is the whole logic of the valid means. Without it, even the pramāṇas are useless. As the Mukuta-saṃhitā says, the consciousness-operation alone is the one reason, established everywhere, in enjoyment or in liberation. The joiner alone is the means. Now the objection presses on memory. "By perception and non-perception," the objector says, "what was made is to be unified; this much is the acceptance of the knower. But what is this? In the unification, the memory alone is engaged." And Abhinavagupta answers with kārikā 5: in memory, that very self-consciousness is the valid means in the self's birth; in the prior-experience-being, it is the proof — that alone, not another. Consider what happens when we remember. The memory seems to bring back a prior object. But it does not bring a *new* thing, a fresh appearance supplied by the memory-time — for memory is of the grasped-grasping nature; it re-grasps what was already grasped. What shines in the memory is the prior experience itself. And it does not now stand as a separate known object — for if it did, we would have the cognition of a known cognition (jñātajñāna), which is not memory at all; and no cognition is known-by-another (as we have shown at length). So, if the prior experience were a separate self-luminous thing, we would have two unconnected experiences, not a memory. The only way the memory is possible is that, at the memory-time, the prior experience itself — being the inner self-consciousness — is what shines. The memory is the prior experience, self-conscious, remembered. And this is the point. The memory is not a second cognition standing over against a first; it is the same self-consciousness, the same knower, continuing. The valid means in memory — and in every cognition — is the self-consciousness of the one knower. It is the knower's own operation, the act by which he knows and re-knows himself. And this is why the one knower is the support of all the powers: knowledge, memory, and removal are all his own self-conscious operation. The valid means is not a thing the knower uses; it is the knower himself, the one who remembers, the same self-consciousness in the self's birth and in the memory — that alone, not another. ---
